• Realistic (1 Hz cardiac wall motion, 0.3 mm amplitude, plus 0.2 mm position noise): force RMSE is ~170 mN. The zero-order-hold  $ \dot{d} = 0 $ model cannot anticipate the periodic motion (Section V-A), so the estimate lags. This is worse than the reported hardware controllers and identifies the cardiac-phase-aware periodic disturbance model (Section V-A, Option B) as essential future work for force-regulation use—not merely an enhancement.

In both force-regulation conditions the peak measured force stays under  $ F_{safe} $ ( $ \sim $0.35 N idealized,  $ \sim $0.43 N with cardiac motion): unlike the stiff reduced model—where the integral force law drove the command toward the cap and an environment-induced  $ b_{t}ij $ impact transient pushed the peak past  $ F_{safe} $—the compliant catheter closes on the wall gently, so the regulation error shows up as a poorly-regulated (not unsafe) force. The hard predicted-force bound caps the controller-induced command throughout, and the position-tracking safety mode holds the bound even more comfortably under the same cardiac motion (Section VI-E, Table IV).
## APPENDIX B
## DERIVATION OF THE LPV STABILITY MARGIN  $ \rho^{\star} $

This appendix proves Proposition 1 in closed form, replacing the “computing the spectral radius” assertion with an explicit Jury analysis. After the exact ZOH discretization (8) the scalar error plant has the constant
$$ A_{d}=\begin{bmatrix}1&\Delta t\\ 0&1\end{bmatrix},\qquad B_{d}(\Lambda_{n})=-\frac{1}{\Lambda_{n}}b,\quad b=\begin{bmatrix}\frac{1}{2}\Delta t^{2}\\ \Delta t\end{bmatrix}. $$

A gain  $ K = [k_1, k_2] $ synthesized at  $ \Lambda_{n,\text{ref}} = 1 $ but acting where the true inertia is  $ \Lambda_{n,\text{true}} $ gives, using  $ B_d(\Lambda_{n,\text{true}}) = (\Lambda_{n,\text{ref}}/\Lambda_{n,\text{true}}) B_d(\Lambda_{n,\text{ref}}) = \rho B_d(\Lambda_{n,\text{ref}}) $ with  $ \rho = \Lambda_{n,\text{ref}}/\Lambda_{n,\text{true}} $,

$$ \begin{align*}A_{cl}(\rho)&=A_{d}-\rho B_{d}(1)K=A_{d}+\rho bK\\&=\begin{bmatrix}1+\frac{1}{2}\rho\Delta t^{2}k_{1}&\Delta t+\frac{1}{2}\rho\Delta t^{2}k_{2}\\ \rho\Delta t k_{1}&1+\rho\Delta t k_{2}\end{bmatrix}.\end{align*} $$
Its characteristic polynomial is  $ \chi(z) = z^{2} - \mathrm{tr}(\rho)z + \det(\rho) $ with
$$ \mathrm{t r}(\rho)=2+\rho\Delta t\big(k_{2}+\textstyle{\frac{1}{2}}\Delta t k_{1}\big), $$
$$ \operatorname*{d e t}(\rho)=1+\rho\Delta t\big(k_{2}-\textstyle{\frac{1}{2}}\Delta t k_{1}\big). $$

(The  $ \rho^{2} $ terms in det cancel because  $ A_{d} $ is unipotent and bK is rank one—the same constant- $ A_{d} $ structure exploited throughout.) By Jury’s criterion a monic second-order  $ \chi $ is Schur iff
$$ \begin{aligned}\left|\det(\rho)\right|<1,\\\chi(1)&=1-\mathrm{tr}+\det>0,\\\chi(-1)&=1+\mathrm{tr}+\det>0.\end{aligned} $$
•  $ z = +1 $:  $ \chi(1) = -\rho \Delta t^2 k_1 > 0 $ for all  $ \rho > 0 $ (since  $ k_1 < 0 $)—never binds.
Substituting (16)–(17) into the three crossings:

- $z = -1: \chi(-1) = 4 + 2\rho\Delta t k_2$, which vanishes at $\rho = -2/(\Delta t k_2) = 2/(\Delta t |k_2|)$ (a real pole reaching $-1$).

- $\left|\det\right| = 1: \det(\rho) < 1$ holds for all $\rho > 0$ (as $k_2 - \frac{1}{2}\Delta t k_1 < 0$), and $\det(\rho) = -1$ at $\rho = 2/(\Delta t |k_2 - \frac{1}{2}\Delta t k_1|)$.
The stability boundary is the smallest positive crossing, giving (14). For the benchmark gains  $ k_1 = -2.04 \times 10^3 $,  $ k_2 = -294.9 $ and  $ \Delta t = 2 $ ms,
$$ \frac{2}{\Delta t\left|k_{2}\right|}=3.39,\qquad\frac{2}{\Delta t\left|k_{2}-\frac{1}{2}\Delta t k_{1}\right|}=3.42, $$

so  $ \rho^* = 3.39 $ (the  $ z = -1 $ flip binds), exactly the value returned by the brute-force spectral-radius sweep over  $ \rho \in [1, 40] $ in catheter_verify.py ( $ \rho_{\text{max}} = 3.39 $). The margin is governed by the velocity gain  $ k_2 $ and the step  $ \Delta t $ alone; with the workspace  $ \rho \in [0.70, 1.0] $ the loop is robustly stable with  $ > 3 \times $ margin (Remark 3).
